title: Given a grid of characters and a word, determine whether the word can be formed by a path of orthogonally adjacent cells, where each cell is used at most once.
shortTitle: Word Search in a Grid (DFS Backtracking)

s1_definition.profdef: Word Search asks whether a target word can be spelled by moving through a grid of letters one step at a time, horizontally or vertically, without reusing a cell. It is solved with depth-first backtracking: from each cell that matches the first letter, you try to extend the match in all four directions, marking cells visited as you go and unmarking them when you back out. The search succeeds the moment a full path spells the word.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India hides a secret approval code across a grid of letters on a security form, and a validator must confirm the code can be traced by stepping between touching cells without landing on the same cell twice. A clerk looks for the first letter anywhere on the grid, then tries to walk to a neighbour holding the second letter, then the third, marking each cell she steps on so she cannot reuse it. If she gets stuck she steps back, unmarks the cell, and tries another direction. If she ever traces the whole code, the form is valid.
s1_definition.oneliner: From each matching start cell, DFS into the four neighbours, marking cells visited and unmarking on backtrack, until the whole word is traced.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Word Search asks whether a target word can be spelled by moving through a grid of letters one step at a time, horizontally or vertically, without reusing a cell. It is solved with depth-first backtracking: from each cell that matches the first letter, you try to extend the match in all four directions, marking cells visited as you go and unmarking them when you back out. The search succeeds the moment a full path spells the word.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India hides a secret approval code across a grid of letters on a security form, and a validator must confirm the code can be traced by stepping between touching cells without landing on the same cell twice. A clerk looks for the first letter anywhere on the grid, then tries to walk to a neighbour holding the second letter, then the third, marking each cell she steps on so she cannot reuse it. If she gets stuck she steps back, unmarks the cell, and tries another direction. If she ever traces the whole code, the form is valid.

**One line to remember:** From each matching start cell, DFS into the four neighbours, marking cells visited and unmarking on backtrack, until the whole word is traced.

sections.s2_technical:
This is backtracking on a grid where the state is your current cell and how many letters of the word you have matched so far. The recursion tries to match the letter at the current word index against the current cell, and if they match it advances to try the next letter from the neighbouring cells.

The base cases are clean. If the word index equals the word length, you have matched every letter, so you return true. If the cell is out of bounds, or its character does not equal the current word letter, you return false for that path. Otherwise you have a match at this cell, so you mark it visited, then recurse into the four neighbours for the next word index: `found = dfs(r+1,c,idx+1) || dfs(r-1,c,idx+1) || dfs(r,c+1,idx+1) || dfs(r,c-1,idx+1);`. The short-circuiting OR means the moment any direction succeeds you stop exploring the rest.

The crucial backtracking step is unmarking the cell after exploring: you temporarily overwrite the cell with a sentinel like a hash character so a path cannot revisit it, then you restore the original character before returning. Restoring is essential, because a different starting path may legitimately need that cell. Forgetting to restore is the classic bug that makes the search wrongly fail. The outer driver loops over all cells and launches the DFS from each, returning true if any start yields a full match.

A senior-level nuance is the complexity and pruning. The worst case is the number of cells times four to the word length, because from each start you branch four ways per letter, though the visited marking and the early character mismatch prune most of that. A strong optional prune is to first count grid letter frequencies and reject immediately if the grid lacks enough of any letter the word needs, and even to reverse the word so the rarer end-letter drives the search. For searching many words at once, you build a trie of the words and DFS the grid once against the trie, which is the Word Search Two optimisation.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India validates that a one-time approval code is correctly embedded as a connected path in a letter grid on a secure form, to defeat tampering. The validator must confirm the code can be traced through adjacent cells without reuse. This is exactly Word Search by DFS backtracking.

Problem 2 — A cell may be used only once within a single traced code, so the search must mark and later unmark cells, and it must try every possible starting position because the code could begin anywhere. The visited-marking with restore and the all-cells outer loop handle both.

In our mini-project we build a `CodePathValidator` with an `exists` method over a character grid. The demo checks a code that is present and one that is not, logging each result.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a three-by-four letter grid and two codes, "BANK" which is present along the top row, and "BOND" which is not.

Step 1: For "BANK", the outer loop finds B at row zero, column zero and launches the DFS with word index zero. B matches, so we mark that cell visited and try neighbours for the letter A.

Step 2: From B we look right to row zero, column one, which holds A, matching the second letter. We mark it and look for N. The cell to the right, row zero column two, holds N, matching. We mark it and look for K.

Step 3: From N we look right to row zero, column three, which holds K, the final letter. Matching advances the index to four, which equals the word length, so we return true up the chain. "BANK" is present.

Step 4: Each cell is restored on the way back out, leaving the grid unchanged for the next query.

Step 5: For "BOND", the outer loop again starts at B. B matches, then we need O among B's neighbours. The neighbours of B are A to the right and X below, neither is O, so this start fails. No other cell holds B, so there is no valid start.

Step 6: The outer loop exhausts all cells without a full trace of "BOND", so we return false. The visited-marking prevented reuse and the restore kept the grid clean between attempts.

```
[2026-10-26 23:36:01] INFO    'BANK' present? true
[2026-10-26 23:36:01] INFO    'BOND' present? false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  grid:            search "BANK"
  B A N K          start (0,0)=B mark
  X Y O S           → right (0,1)=A → right (0,2)=N → right (0,3)=K
  Z W T A           idx==len → true  (restore cells on unwind)

  search "BOND"
  start (0,0)=B → need O; neighbours A,X → no match → false
  no other B → overall false
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Word Search (Grid DFS Backtracking) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  DFS backtracking with in-place visited sentinel + restore    │
  │  Short-circuit OR over 4 directions                          │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: CodePathValidator only checks path existence              │
  │  O: swap DFS for trie-driven multi-word search (Word Search II)│
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           CodePathValidator           │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + exists(grid, word): boolean        │  O(cells · 4^len) worst
  │  - dfs(grid, r, c, word, idx): boolean│  match/mark/recurse/restore
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      Pre:  grid non-empty
      Post: true iff a non-reusing adjacent path spells word

  ── State Diagram: DFS cell ──────────────────────────────

  [idx == len] ──→ true (done)
  [out of bounds / mismatch] ──→ false
  [match] ──→ mark '#', recurse 4-dir, restore, return found

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. exists: for each start cell → dfs(r,c,word,0)
  2.   match → mark; try 4 neighbours at idx+1
  3.   restore cell; return OR of directions
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Word Search asks whether a target word can be spelled by moving through a grid of letters one orthogonal step at a time without reusing any cell. I solve it with depth-first backtracking where the state is my current cell and how many letters of the word I have matched. The recursion matches the current word letter against the current cell, and when they match it advances to try the next letter from the four neighbouring cells.

The base cases are simple: if the word index reaches the word length I have matched everything and return true, and if the cell is out of bounds or its letter does not match the current word letter I return false for that path. When a cell matches, the critical two steps are marking it visited, usually by overwriting it in place with a sentinel character so no path revisits it, and then after exploring all four directions, restoring the original character before returning. That restore is essential because a different starting path may legitimately need that cell, and forgetting it is the classic bug. I use a short-circuiting OR across the four directions so the moment one direction succeeds I stop, and an outer loop launches the search from every cell because the word could begin anywhere.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to validate that a one-time approval code is correctly embedded as a connected path in a letter grid on a secure form, which helps defeat tampering. The visited-marking prevented reusing a cell within one trace, the restore kept the grid clean between attempts, and the all-cells outer loop handled codes that could start anywhere.

The senior-level point I make is about the exponential worst case, which is the number of cells times four to the word length, and the pruning that tames it. I mention counting grid letter frequencies to reject immediately when the grid lacks a needed letter, and even reversing the word so its rarer end-letter drives the search. I also note that when searching many words at once, the right approach is to build a trie of all the words and DFS the grid a single time against the trie, which is the Word Search Two optimisation, so I show I know how the problem scales from one word to many.
